stem: An equity index is at 100 and has a continuously compounded dividend yield of 1.5%. The continuously compounded risk-free rate is 4%. The no-arbitrage six-month forward price is closest to:

rationale.B: Incorrect. 102.02 = 100 × e^(0.04 × 0.5) ignores the dividend yield.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 100.75 = 100 × e^(0.015 × 0.5) uses the dividend yield in place of the net carry rate.

stem: A forward contract on a non-dividend-paying share is quoted below its no-arbitrage price. An arbitrageur should most likely:
options: borrow, buy the share and go short the forward
short-sell the share, lend the proceeds and go long the forward
go long the forward and hold it unhedged until expiration
explanation: An underpriced forward should be bought, and the asset sold short with the proceeds lent at the risk-free rate (reverse cash-and-carry). At expiration the forward delivers the share to close the short position.

rationale.A: Incorrect. This cash-and-carry trade profits when the forward is overpriced, not underpriced.
rationale.B: Correct. Reverse cash-and-carry locks in the gap between the no-arbitrage price and the cheap market forward.
rationale.C: Incorrect. An unhedged long forward is a speculative position, not a riskless arbitrage.

stem: A non-dividend-paying share trades at USD 60 and the annual risk-free rate is 3%. A dealer offers a one-year forward at USD 63. The riskless profit per share at expiration from the appropriate arbitrage is closest to:
explanation: F0 = 60 × 1.03 = 61.80. The market forward of 63 is overpriced, so a cash-and-carry earns 63 − 61.80 = 1.20 at expiration.

rationale.A: Incorrect. 3.00 = 63 − 60 ignores the cost of financing the share purchase.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 1.17 is the present value of the profit today; the question asks for the profit at expiration.
